name: Topical clindamycin

lead: Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic gel, lotion or foam used for mild to moderate acne. People use it to cut down red, inflamed pimples and get a clearer complexion.

It reduces acne bacteria on the skin. It is usually combined with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, and reference sources report the combination works better than clindamycin alone. Randomised trials from the 1990s and 2000s compared clindamycin and benzoyl peroxide gels with each ingredient and with plain vehicle.

paras: It is applied to the affected skin as part of a prescribed routine, most often in a combination product with benzoyl peroxide. Pairing is intended to counter resistant bacteria. Improvement in inflamed lesions is typically judged over several weeks.

Dryness, burning, itching, peeling and contact dermatitis are reported in over 10% of users. Antibiotic resistance is a recognised concern, which is why it is rarely used alone. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Prescribed clindamycin gel or lotion reduces acne bacteria on the skin, so fewer inflamed pimples form and the complexion looks clearer. It is usually used with benzoyl peroxide and is well studied in clinical trials.

lead: Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic lotion, gel, solution or foam applied to the skin for mild to moderate acne. By reducing the acne-associated bacterium Cutibacterium acnes and the inflammation around it, it helps clear red, inflamed pimples, which in turn reduces the marks and scarring risk that picked or long-lasting breakouts leave behind.[1][2]

It is most often prescribed in a combination: with benzoyl peroxide (brands such as BenzaClin, Duac, Acanya and Onexton), with tretinoin (Ziana in the US), or in a newer fixed-dose triple gel that adds adapalene.[1][3][4] The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline gives strong recommendations to topical antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids, and includes a good-practice statement on combining topical therapies with different mechanisms of action.[5]

Clindamycin is a semisynthetic derivative of the natural antibiotic lincomycin. Its synthesis was announced in 1966 and it has been on the market since 1968.[1] The topical form is a prodrug (clindamycin phosphate) that the skin converts to active clindamycin; absorption through the skin is small.[3][6] Bacterial resistance is a recognised concern, which is why dermatology references usually describe it as one part of a combination rather than a stand-alone long-term treatment.[7][2]
infobox: Cleocin T, Dalacin T; combinations BenzaClin, Duac, Acanya, Onexton, Ziana[1][3]
Clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide approved in the US in December 2000[3]
Prescription-only (US, Canada, UK, Australia); generics available[1]

paras: Topical clindamycin phosphate treats mild to moderate acne and comes as a solution, gel, lotion or foam.[1] Wikipedia notes that clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide performs better than clindamycin alone, and that over the long term it performed similarly to salicylic acid plus benzoyl peroxide.[1][8] Combination products include clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide (BenzaClin, Duac, Acanya, Onexton) and, in the US, clindamycin with tretinoin (Ziana).[1][3]

Wikipedia's acne article describes benzoyl peroxide as a first-line option that, unlike antibiotics, does not appear to generate resistance, and says dermatologists generally use topical antibiotics as part of combination therapy; the Global Alliance to Improve Outcomes in Acne advises against using topical and oral antibiotics together.[2]

Wikipedia states that tretinoin formulations are mostly incompatible with benzoyl peroxide, and its clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide article adds that topical retinoids may be inactivated by benzoyl peroxide or increase its irritant effect.[3]

Topical clindamycin also appears in reviews of other inflammatory skin conditions. A Cochrane review of rosacea interventions reported that topical clindamycin phosphate combined with tretinoin was not considered effective compared with placebo, while topical metronidazole outperformed placebo in papulopustular rosacea.[9] Reviews of hidradenitis suppurativa and perioral dermatitis also discuss topical antibiotic options, and a 21-person split-face study compared photodynamic therapy with topical clindamycin for perioral dermatitis.[10][11][12]

Clindamycin has been supplied as a solution, lotion, gel and foam. A 1985 randomised trial compared Cleocin T solution with lotion, and a 2005 multicentre randomised trial compared a 1% foam with a 1% gel and vehicle foam.[13][14] Research prototypes such as clindamycin-loaded nanofiber patches have also been described.[15]

Wikipedia lists brand names including Cleocin, Clinacin and Dalacin for clindamycin generally, and BenzaClin, Duac and Acanya for the benzoyl peroxide combinations.[1] Onexton, a 1.2%/3.75% clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gel, was the subject of patent litigation: Wikipedia reports that the US patent issued in October 2012, that Dow Pharmaceutical Sciences and Valeant sued Taro in 2016 over a generic filing, and that Perrigo settled its own litigation.[3]

Topical effects include dryness, burning, itching, scaling, peeling, redness and contact dermatitis, reported in over 10% of users.[1] For the benzoyl peroxide combination, Wikipedia adds that benzoyl peroxide bleaches hair and fabrics, that the gel may increase photosensitivity, and that irritation can be reduced by avoiding harsh cleansers and using sunscreen.[3]

Systemic clindamycin raises the risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis, and pseudomembranous colitis can be life-threatening; those figures concern systemic use rather than skin application.[1] Wikipedia notes that clinical studies have shown some systemic absorption of topically applied clindamycin, with reports of diarrhoea, bloody diarrhoea and colitis, and that the reports of anaphylaxis came from uncontrolled personal accounts whose cause is hard to attribute.[3]

A 1989 crossover study of 12 healthy male volunteers applying topical clindamycin to the face found an absolute bioavailability of about 1.7% for Cleocin T and no appreciable accumulation with repeated dosing.[6] The combination gel is not recommended for people with allergy to clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide or lincomycin, or with a history of regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis or antibiotic-associated colitis.[3]

Wikipedia states that studies of clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide in pregnancy and breastfeeding have not been performed, and that limited data on topical clindamycin and benzoyl peroxide have shown no safety problems.[3]

Clindamycin binds the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and inhibits protein synthesis; it is mainly bacteriostatic, and more potent than lincomycin.[1] In acne it acts on C. acnes, which Wikipedia describes as playing a role in the development of the condition.[3]

Research on the immune side of acne reports that C. acnes triggers inflammatory signalling through Toll-like receptor 2 on macrophages around affected follicles, one explanation for why bacteria-targeting treatments can also reduce inflammation.[16]

Clindamycin phosphate is an inactive prodrug that is rapidly hydrolysed to clindamycin; after four weeks of application of the combination gel, about 0.043% of the applied dose was found in blood, according to Wikipedia.[3]

Resistance is a recognised concern. Inducible macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B resistance, mediated by erm genes, can be detected in the lab with the D-test, and combining clindamycin with macrolides is generally avoided because of antagonism.[1] Topical erythromycin may antagonise clindamycin in laboratory studies.[3]

A 16-week trial in 79 patients aged 13 to 30 found that clindamycin-resistant C. acnes counts rose by more than 1,600% with clindamycin gel alone, a rise not seen with the clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gel; lesion reductions correlated with falls in resistant bacteria.[17]

Clindamycin was made in 1966 by replacing a hydroxyl group on lincomycin with chlorine, and the synthesis was announced by B.J. Magerlein, R.D. Birkenmeyer and F. Kagan at the 1966 Interscience Conference on Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy; it has been on the market since 1968.[1] Topical formulations were already being compared in acne trials by the mid-1980s, and combination gels with benzoyl peroxide were studied through the 1990s and approved in the US in December 2000.[3][13][18]
Wikipedia reports that clindamycin appears on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and was the 149th most prescribed drug in the US in 2023.[1]
Topical clindamycin is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the UK and Australia, and is available as a generic.[1]

On T Nation, a member asking about isotretinoin described a year of oral minocycline plus a clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide cream and a clindamycin/tretinoin gel prescribed by a dermatologist, and another member discussing steroid-related acne reported that minocycline plus clindamycin gel had worked for them.[19][20]
Both posts describe clindamycin as part of a dermatologist-prescribed regimen rather than a self-sourced product.

A pooled analysis of two double-blind, vehicle-controlled trials applied one of four gels nightly for 11 weeks (334 completers). All three active gels beat vehicle, and the clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide combination was significantly better than each component for global improvement and inflammatory lesion reduction, with tolerance not significantly different from vehicle.[18]

A 2010 meta-analysis of 23 studies with 7,309 patients compared benzoyl peroxide, clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide/salicylic acid and benzoyl peroxide/clindamycin. At 2 to 4 weeks, mean inflammatory lesion reductions were 40.7% for benzoyl peroxide/clindamycin and 21.5% for clindamycin alone; at 10 to 12 weeks they were 55.6% and 45.9% respectively, with benzoyl peroxide/clindamycin and benzoyl peroxide/salicylic acid similar. The authors reported that benzoyl peroxide/clindamycin was only slightly better than benzoyl peroxide alone and superior to clindamycin alone.[8]

The 16-week randomised trial comparing clindamycin 1%/benzoyl peroxide 5% gel with matching clindamycin gel found larger reductions in total lesions, inflammatory lesions and comedones with the combination (P up to 0.046).[17]

Two trials compared clindamycin gel with nicotinamide gel: a 76-patient, 8-week trial of 4% nicotinamide versus 1% clindamycin found comparable results, with improvement in 82% versus 68%, and a 60-patient trial of 5% nicotinamide versus 2% clindamycin reported no significant difference in the Acne Severity Index.[21][22] A 12-week randomised study examined benzoyl peroxide 5%/clindamycin 1% gel with and without adapalene, and a multicentre randomised trial examined clindamycin 1% gel.[23][24]

The phase II trial of the triple combination (clindamycin 1.2%, benzoyl peroxide 3.1%, adapalene 0.15%) enrolled 741 participants aged 9 and older with moderate-to-severe acne for 12 weeks. Treatment success was 52.5% with the triple gel versus 8.1% with vehicle and 27.8% to 30.5% with the three two-ingredient gels; inflammatory lesion reductions were 29.9 versus 19.6 to 26.8, and most adverse events were mild to moderate.[4] A 2024 report summarised six participants from two phase 3 trials, all of whom had more than 70% lesion reduction at week 12.[25] Registered phase 3 trials include an adapalene-clindamycin gel (n=1,617) and clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gels (n=1,315 and n=708).[26][27][28]

lore.intro: Topical clindamycin is discussed in appearance forums as the Rx step dermatologists try before or alongside isotretinoin, usually in a combination with benzoyl peroxide or tretinoin.[19][20]
